title: The Four Financial Statements & Articulation (CMA P1-A · feeds FAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — two balanced ledgers are not one company

Illustrative control totals: the MBG general ledger is $12,480,000.00 and the Riverton general ledger is $16,920,000.00; both were reported as balanced in the Q1 close analysis. Those figures are control evidence, not permission to combine the entities. MBG and Riverton have different bank accounts, reciprocal intercompany accounts, and separate reporting responsibilities. Before preparing any statement, select one entity, one reporting date, one accounting basis, and one exact trial balance.

A balanced trial balance proves that posted debits equal posted credits. It does not prove that accounts are correctly classified, that all transactions were recorded, or that the reporting period is closed. MBG's Q1 remained open with 12 items even though the ledgers balanced. Financial statement preparation therefore begins with the adjusted trial balance and ends with articulation checks across four statements.

Concept — four views of one accounting system

The balance sheet reports assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time. Its governing equation is Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Cash, receivables, and construction in progress are assets because they represent controlled resources with expected future benefit. Accounts payable, retainage payable, and notes payable are liabilities because they are present obligations. Equity is the residual interest.

The income statement reports revenues, expenses, gains, and losses over a period. Net income measures performance under accrual accounting; it is not the change in cash. Construction revenue can be recognized before billing or collection, while equipment purchases may use cash without becoming immediate expense.

The statement of changes in equity reconciles beginning equity to ending equity. For a simple corporation: Beginning retained earnings + net income − dividends = ending retained earnings. Additional paid-in capital, owner contributions, distributions, and accumulated other comprehensive income appear when applicable. A closing entry transfers temporary-account results into retained earnings; it does not create the underlying profit.

The statement of cash flows explains the change in cash through operating, investing, and financing activities. Under the indirect method, operating cash flow begins with net income and adjusts for noncash items and changes in operating assets and liabilities. Buying equipment is generally investing; borrowing principal is financing; interest classification follows the applicable reporting framework and policy.

Articulation checkpoints

  • Ending cash on the cash-flow statement equals balance-sheet cash.
  • Net income flows from the income statement into retained earnings, subject to dividends and other equity changes.
  • Ending retained earnings equals the equity statement and balance sheet.
  • Every balance-sheet account derives from the adjusted trial balance.
  • The cash-flow change plus beginning cash equals ending cash.

Worked example — build all four statements

The following compact trial balance is illustrative; the MBG and Riverton totals above are control totals, but the source does not provide a complete account-by-account adjusted TB suitable for publication here.

AccountDebitCredit
Cash$180,000—
Accounts receivable$260,000—
WIP/CIP$420,000—
Equipment, net$140,000—
Accounts payable—$220,000
Debt—$300,000
Common stock—$200,000
Beginning retained earnings—$120,000
Revenue—$600,000
Cost of revenue$420,000—
Operating expense$20,000—
Total$1,440,000$1,440,000

The income statement reports $600,000 revenue minus $420,000 cost of revenue minus $20,000 operating expense, producing illustrative net income of $160,000. With no dividends in the displayed trial balance, ending retained earnings are $120,000 + $160,000 = $280,000.

The balance sheet reports assets of $1,000,000: cash $180,000, receivables $260,000, WIP $420,000, and net equipment $140,000. Liabilities are $520,000 and ending equity is $480,000: common stock $200,000 plus retained earnings $280,000. Liabilities plus equity equal $1,000,000. The closing process removes the temporary revenue and expense accounts while transferring their $160,000 net result into retained earnings.

Assume beginning cash was an illustrative $110,000. Cash increased $70,000. One possible cash-flow reconciliation is $90,000 operating inflow, $50,000 equipment purchase, and $30,000 financing inflow: $90,000 − $50,000 + $30,000 = $70,000. Under the indirect method, operating cash flow would begin with $160,000 net income and explain the $70,000 net reduction from noncash and working-capital adjustments to reach $90,000 operating cash.

The point is not to reverse-engineer cash from a desired answer. Each change must be supported by comparative balance sheets and transaction detail. The articulation equations then detect omissions: if cash-flow ending cash is $175,000 while the balance sheet shows $180,000, the package has a $5,000 unresolved error.

Apply the method to MBG

  1. Export the MBG adjusted TB from JCS for the exact cutoff; do not call JCS Ledgerline 100.
  2. Compute true ending balances from beginning plus YTD debits minus YTD credits because “Acct Ending Bal” is not cumulative.
  3. Map exact accounts to statement lines; never use substring matches.
  4. Prepare the income statement and equity rollforward before finalizing the balance sheet.
  5. Build the cash-flow statement from comparative balances and supported noncash details.
  6. Run articulation checks and document every difference to $0.00.
  7. Repeat independently for Riverton; consolidation is a later layer with eliminations.

A bank tie is stronger evidence for cash than an internally balanced GL. MBG account 102.1 must tie to its First Regional Bank statement, while Riverton account 102 ties to its own statement. Entity segregation is an assertion about ownership, not merely presentation.

Common construction-package traps

Classifying WIP as current does not mean it is cash-equivalent. It must be evaluated within the operating cycle and supported by job detail. A large contract asset is not the same as accounts receivable because the right may remain conditional on something other than time. Retainage can also require separate presentation or disclosure depending on the facts. These distinctions affect current ratio, working capital, and cash-flow analysis even when total assets are unchanged.

Contra accounts must remain connected to their related assets. Accumulated depreciation reduces property and equipment; an allowance reduces the related receivable. Netting unrelated debit and credit balances can make a trial balance appear concise while violating presentation rules. Likewise, offsetting intercompany accounts belongs to consolidation after reciprocity is proved, not to the separate MBG or Riverton statements.

Comparative statements add another control. Each ending balance becomes the next period's beginning balance, subject to supported retrospective adjustments. If opening retained earnings does not equal the prior issued ending balance, identify the restatement, prior-period correction, or data error explicitly. Never plug the difference into current income.

Finally, distinguish transactions from classifications. Paying AP changes cash and a liability but not current expense. Depreciation changes expense and a contra asset without using cash. Closing a home transfers WIP to cost of sales and recognizes the related balance-sheet relief. Every event must appear consistently across the statements it affects.

Extended worked example — comparative balance sheets to a complete cash-flow statement

The first illustration built statements forward from one trial balance. Exam questions more often run the other direction: they hand you two balance sheets plus an income statement and require the statement of cash flows. The following illustrative MBG data works that direction end to end, with every intermediate figure shown rather than asserted.

AccountBeginningEndingChange
Cash$210,000$288,000+$78,000
Accounts receivable$260,000$315,000+$55,000
WIP/CIP$420,000$468,000+$48,000
Equipment, gross$300,000$370,000+$70,000
Accumulated depreciation$(60,000)$(75,000)$(15,000)
Total assets$1,130,000$1,366,000+$236,000
Accounts payable$220,000$244,000+$24,000
Retainage payable$40,000$52,000+$12,000
Notes payable$300,000$350,000+$50,000
Common stock$200,000$220,000+$20,000
Additional paid-in capital$100,000$130,000+$30,000
Retained earnings$270,000$370,000+$100,000
Total liabilities and equity$1,130,000$1,366,000+$236,000

Supporting facts for the period: net income was $160,000; depreciation expense was $45,000; equipment that originally cost $50,000 with $30,000 of accumulated depreciation was sold for $26,000 cash; $120,000 of equipment was purchased for cash; $90,000 was borrowed on a note and $40,000 of principal was repaid; stock was issued for $50,000 cash, of which $20,000 was par and $30,000 was additional paid-in capital; and $60,000 of dividends were declared and paid.

Step 1 — separate the noncash and nonoperating pieces

The equipment sold had a carrying amount of $50,000 minus $30,000, or $20,000. Proceeds of $26,000 therefore produced a gain of $26,000 minus $20,000, or $6,000. That gain is already inside the $160,000 of net income, so the operating section must remove it; the cash it represents belongs in investing, and it belongs there at the full $26,000 of proceeds.

Step 2 — roll the long-lived asset accounts

Gross equipment: $300,000 plus $120,000 purchased minus $50,000 disposed equals $370,000. Accumulated depreciation: $60,000 plus $45,000 of expense minus $30,000 removed on disposal equals $75,000. Net equipment moves from $240,000 to $295,000, a $55,000 increase, even though $120,000 of cash was spent. Neither the $370,000 nor the $75,000 ever appears on the cash-flow statement; only the $120,000 outflow and the $26,000 inflow do.

Step 3 — operating activities, indirect method

LineAmountWhy
Net income$160,000Starting point
Add depreciation+$45,000Expense that used no cash
Subtract gain on sale−$6,000Nonoperating; its cash appears in investing
Increase in accounts receivable−$55,000Revenue recognized but not collected
Increase in WIP−$48,000Cost incurred and capitalized, not yet expensed
Increase in accounts payable+$24,000Cost incurred but not yet paid
Increase in retainage payable+$12,000Obligation incurred but withheld from payment
Net cash from operating activities$132,000160 + 45 − 6 − 55 − 48 + 24 + 12

Step 4 — investing and financing activities

Investing: $26,000 of proceeds from the equipment sale less $120,000 paid for new equipment equals negative $94,000. Financing: $90,000 borrowed, less $40,000 of principal repaid, plus $50,000 of stock proceeds, less $60,000 of dividends paid, equals positive $40,000. Note that the note activity is presented gross. Showing a single net $50,000 borrowing line would conceal $130,000 of gross financing activity that lenders and sureties analyze.

Step 5 — prove the articulation

Net change in cash is $132,000 minus $94,000 plus $40,000, or $78,000. Beginning cash of $210,000 plus $78,000 equals ending cash of $288,000, exactly the balance-sheet figure. Retained earnings rolls $270,000 plus $160,000 minus $60,000 to $370,000. Total assets of $288,000 + $315,000 + $468,000 + $370,000 − $75,000 = $1,366,000 equal total liabilities and equity of $244,000 + $52,000 + $350,000 + $220,000 + $130,000 + $370,000 = $1,366,000. All four statements now agree.

Statement of changes in equity

ComponentBeginningAdditionsReductionsEnding
Common stock$200,000$20,000 issued—$220,000
Additional paid-in capital$100,000$30,000 issued—$130,000
Retained earnings$270,000$160,000 net income$(60,000) dividends$370,000
Total equity$570,000$210,000$(60,000)$720,000

Equity increased $150,000. That figure is independently confirmed by the transaction logic: $160,000 of net income minus $60,000 of dividends plus $50,000 of stock issuance equals $150,000. Two routes to the same number is what articulation means in practice.

Traps that cost the mark

Trap — investing reports the proceeds, not the gain

Trap: the operating section removes the $6,000 gain, but investing reports the $26,000 of proceeds. Putting the $6,000 gain into investing instead of the proceeds gives investing cash of negative $114,000 rather than negative $94,000 — a $20,000 error that leaves ending cash $20,000 short of the balance sheet. The rule: reverse the gain or loss in operating, then show the entire cash received in investing.

Trap — the direction of a working-capital change

Trap: an increase in an operating asset such as receivables or WIP is a use of cash and is subtracted; an increase in an operating liability such as payables or retainage is a source and is added. Reversing the AR and WIP signs in this problem swings operating cash by twice $55,000 plus twice $48,000, or $206,000 — from $132,000 to $338,000. Check the direction against the economics rather than a memorized sign: MBG billed customers $55,000 more than it collected, so that cash is not in the bank.

Trap — declared versus paid

Trap: only dividends paid are a financing outflow. Had MBG declared $60,000 but paid only $45,000, retained earnings would still fall $60,000, financing would show $(45,000), and a $15,000 dividends-payable liability would appear on the balance sheet. The equity rollforward and the cash-flow statement then use different numbers from the same event, and both are correct.

Trap — depreciation is not a source of cash

Trap: adding back $45,000 of depreciation does not mean depreciation generated $45,000. The add-back reverses a deduction that never consumed cash. An entity with no revenue and $45,000 of depreciation has a $45,000 net loss, a zero net result after the add-back, and no cash at all.

Trap — noncash investing and financing

Trap: acquiring equipment by directly assuming a note is a noncash transaction. It never enters the three cash sections and instead requires supplemental disclosure. If MBG had bought $120,000 of equipment with seller financing rather than cash, investing would be positive $26,000, financing would be $100,000, net change in cash would be $258,000, and the balance sheet would be unchanged. Recording the same event through the cash sections would report $120,000 of cash movement that never occurred.

The same period by the direct method

The indirect method explains why operating cash differs from net income. The direct method shows the receipts and payments themselves. Both must produce the same $132,000. Assume MBG's illustrative income statement for the period is revenue $1,400,000, cost of revenue $1,050,000, operating expenses $174,000 (including the $45,000 of depreciation), interest expense $22,000, and the $6,000 gain on the equipment sale. Because this illustrative entity is taxed as a pass-through, there is no entity-level income tax: $1,400,000 − $1,050,000 − $174,000 − $22,000 + $6,000 = $160,000 of net income.

Direct-method lineDerivationAmount
Cash collected from customers$1,400,000 revenue − $55,000 increase in AR$1,345,000
Cash paid for construction costs$1,050,000 cost of revenue + $48,000 WIP increase − $24,000 AP increase − $12,000 retainage increase$(1,062,000)
Cash paid for operating expenses$174,000 − $45,000 depreciation$(129,000)
Cash paid for interestNo change in accrued interest$(22,000)
Net cash from operating activities$1,345,000 − $1,062,000 − $129,000 − $22,000$132,000

Read the construction-cost line carefully. Costs incurred were $1,050,000 charged to cost of revenue plus the $48,000 that stayed in WIP, or $1,098,000. Of that, $36,000 was still unpaid at period end through the increases in accounts payable and retainage payable, so only $1,062,000 left the bank. The gain on sale appears nowhere in the direct method at all, because no operating cash was received for it.

Trap — the direct method still requires an indirect reconciliation

Trap: choosing the direct method does not remove the net-income-to-operating-cash reconciliation; it relocates it. Candidates who present only receipts and payments and skip the reconciliation lose the presentation mark even when every number is right.

Diagnostic — locating an articulation break

Suppose the package reports ending cash of $283,000 on the cash-flow statement while the balance sheet shows $288,000. The $5,000 gap is not a rounding artifact and must not be plugged. Work the checks in order: does beginning cash tie to the prior issued statement; do the three sections sum to the reported net change; does retained earnings roll to the balance sheet; does each balance-sheet change have a documented cause. In this illustration the $5,000 would surface as a missing financing line or a working-capital change computed off a pre-adjustment trial balance. An articulation check is valuable precisely because it forces two independently prepared statements to collide.

CPA Crossover — FAR

FAR adds classification, disclosure, and presentation detail: current versus noncurrent, discontinued operations, other comprehensive income, noncash financing and investing disclosures, and statement format. The same articulation logic remains central. A question may provide comparative balance sheets and an income statement, then require cash flows; solve by identifying account changes, classifying their causes, and excluding noncash transactions from the main cash-flow sections.

Practice and recap

When reviewing a package, ask four separate questions: does the balance sheet balance, does the income statement reflect the period, does equity roll correctly, and does cash reconcile to independent evidence? Then ask whether all four agree with one another. A balanced statement can still be wrong; articulation makes separate errors collide.

Recap: the four statements are not independent reports. Net income changes equity, transactions change balance-sheet accounts, and the cash-flow statement explains one balance-sheet change. Start from an adjusted, entity-specific trial balance and require exact articulation before relying on any total.

flashcards.front: What does a balanced trial balance prove?
flashcards.back: Only that posted debits equal posted credits; it does not prove completeness, cutoff, valuation, or classification.

flashcards.front: How does net income articulate with equity?
flashcards.back: Net income increases retained earnings, subject to dividends, distributions, and other equity changes.

flashcards.front: What must ending cash on the cash-flow statement equal?
flashcards.back: The balance-sheet cash balance for the same entity and date.

flashcards.front: Why can net income differ from operating cash flow?
flashcards.back: Accruals, noncash expenses, and working-capital changes separate performance recognition from cash timing.

flashcards.front: What are the MBG and Riverton GL control totals?
flashcards.back: MBG $12,480,000.00 and Riverton $16,920,000.00; keep the entities separate.

flashcards.front: Which statement reconciles beginning to ending retained earnings?
flashcards.back: The statement of changes in equity.

flashcards.front: What is the strongest evidence for a bank balance?
flashcards.back: The bank statement and reconciliation, not merely a balanced GL.

questions.q: Illustrative revenue is $600,000, cost of revenue $420,000, and operating expense $20,000. Net income is:
Beginning retained earnings are $120,000, net income is $160,000, and dividends are $30,000. Ending retained earnings are:
Which event is generally an investing cash flow?
questions.explain: Purchasing a long-lived asset is generally an investing activity.

questions.q: A trial balance is balanced. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.explain: Arithmetic equality does not establish the other financial-statement assertions.

questions.q: Ending cash per the cash-flow statement is $175,000 and balance-sheet cash is $180,000. What should happen?
choices: Investigate and resolve the $5,000 articulation error
questions.explain: The statements must articulate for the same entity and date; an unexplained difference is an error.

questions.q: Which statement reports financial position at a point in time?
questions.explain: The balance sheet presents assets, liabilities, and equity at the reporting date.

questions.q: Why must MBG and Riverton statements be prepared separately first?
choices: They are distinct entities with separate accounts and ownership assertions
questions.explain: Entity-specific ledgers and bank accounts must be correct before any consolidation layer.
